answer_text: A controller has 1 month to act on a data subject's request, and that period may be extended by 2 further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests, under Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation).
The prohibitions of the AI Act apply from 2 February 2025, and the Regulation applies from 2 August 2026.
Providers must publish the average number of monthly active recipients at least once every 6 months, calculated as an average over the period of the past 6 months.
The trader must deliver the goods without undue delay, and in any event, not more than 30 days after the day on which the contract is entered into.
A person aged 12 or over is presumed to be of sufficient age and maturity to have such understanding, in Scotland, under the Data Protection Act 2018.

The pre-ticked box is not valid consent, and the letter-only withdrawal is not acceptable. 
This is based on [1], which states that pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not constitute consent. 
According to [3.2] and [3.3], the request for consent must be presented in a manner which is clearly distinguishable from other matters and the withdrawal of consent should be as easy to withdraw as to give consent. 
The requirement for a signed letter to withdraw consent, as stated in the terms, does not meet this condition. 
Additionally, [1] and [32] emphasize the need for a clear affirmative act for consent, which a pre-ticked box does not provide.

The university lab's use is not caught by the prohibition, but the retailer's use is. 
This is based on Article 5 (f) of the AI Act, as seen in [1] and [2], which prohibits the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions, except where the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. 
The university lab's use for scientific research does not fall under the exceptions, but it also does not explicitly fall under the prohibited areas, as stated in [4], the prohibition targets systems used to detect the emotional state of individuals in situations related to the workplace and education, implying a more direct application or impact. 
In contrast, the retailer's use directly targets staff mood in the workplace, clearly falling under the prohibition. 
Additionally, as noted in [3] and [4], the use of AI systems to detect emotional states can lead to discriminatory outcomes and intrusion into rights and freedoms, which supports the prohibition in the context of the retailer's use.

The online platform must give the user access to an effective internal complaint-handling system to challenge the removal, for at least six months, from the day the user is informed about the decision, and the challenge must be free of charge. 
This is based on Article 20 of the Digital Services Act, as stated in [1] and [2], which specify the conditions for the internal complaint-handling system, including the period and cost. 
The period of at least six months starts on the day the user is informed about the decision, as stated in [2]. 
The internal complaint-handling system must be easy to access, user-friendly, and enable the submission of sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated complaints, as stated in [3] and [5]. 
The user can lodge a complaint electronically and free of charge, as stated in [1].

The platform company had 2 months to notify the Commission, and the maximum fine for failing to do so is 1% of its total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year. 
This is based on Article 3(3) of the Digital Markets Act, [1], which states that the company shall notify the Commission within 2 months after the thresholds are met. 
The fine is specified in Article 30, [2], which states that the Commission may impose a fine not exceeding 1% of the undertaking's total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year for failing to notify the Commission according to Article 3(3). 
Additionally, [4] confirms that the company must notify the Commission when a further core platform service meets the thresholds, and [3] provides further context for the fine, although the 1% limit applies in this case.

The consumer can no longer use the short-term right to reject, as the time limit of 30 days has passed. 
This is based on [2], section 22, subsection (1), which states that the short-term right to reject is lost if the time limit passes without the consumer exercising it. 
The time limit is defined in [2], section 22, subsection (3), as 30 days after certain conditions are met, including delivery of the goods. 
The next remedy is likely to be a request for repair or replacement, as stated in [5], section 22, subsection (6). 
According to [3], section 19, subsection (14), the consumer does not have to prove the fault existed at delivery, as goods that do not conform to the contract within six months of delivery are presumed not to have conformed to it on the day of delivery, unless it is established that they did conform or the application of this rule is incompatible with the nature of the goods or the failure.

Digital Markets Act: 45 million monthly active end users
The Digital Markets Act requires, alongside the 45 million monthly active end users figure, at least 10 000 yearly active business users.

AI Act: 7 % 
Digital Services Act: 6 % 
Digital Markets Act: 10 % 
The values are directly comparable and the fine is highest for the Digital Markets Act.

The AI Act uses the definition of 'personal data' from Regulation (EU) 2016/679. This definition is referred to in [3] and [5], which state that 'personal data' means personal data as defined in Article 4, point (1), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679. The exact wording of the definition is not provided in the given evidence passages, but it is referenced in Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act) [1] and Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2022/868 (Data Governance Act) [5], as well as in Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act) [3].

Data Protection Act 2018 - 2018: NOT_FOUND
EU GDPR - 2016: NOT_FOUND
The values are not directly comparable.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act) - general case: 15 days
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation): 72 hours
The deadline under the GDPR (72 hours) is shorter than the deadline under the AI Act (15 days).
